source_claims.statement: C is a general-purpose language created in 1972 by Dennis Ritchie for relatively direct CPU architecture access.
C is used for operating systems, kernels, drivers, protocol stacks, supercomputers, microcontrollers and embedded systems.
C evolved from B/New B in the context of Unix development and reimplemented the Unix kernel.
C is static, weakly enforced/typed, manifest and nominal.
C provides static, automatic and dynamic storage with manual management.
C combines low-level access with portability through standardized semantics.
The preprocessor provides macros/inclusion/conditional compilation and libraries extend the small core.
Array and pointer semantics are tightly coupled; unchecked bounds are both powerful and risky.
C evolved from K&R through C89/C90/C95/C99/C11/C17/C23 and C2Y/C29.
Embedded C addresses fixed-point arithmetic, named address spaces and hardware I/O.
C is used in systems, games, servers, CGI history and computational libraries.
C interoperates with assembly and higher-level languages and implements other language runtimes.
C has memory, type-safety, runtime-checking, aliasing, ABI, preprocessing and error-handling limitations.
Coding standards, analysis tools and hardware capabilities mitigate subsets of C risks.
C influenced a broad family of programming and hardware-description languages.

value.name: Container environment model

value.meaning: Multiple containers collectively share a common operating-system kernel.

value.name: Container portability model
value.expression: Bundled application environment + compatible runtime -> cloud/non-cloud deployment across vendors
value.meaning: Containerization is framed as allowing applications to run across cloud or non-cloud environments regardless of vendor.

value.name: OCI interoperability model
value.expression: Standard image + standard runtime + standard distribution -> interoperability across implementations/tools
value.meaning: OCI specifications are intended to make images and runtimes interoperable across implementations and tools.

value.name: Container runtime lifecycle
value.expression: Runtime configuration -> execution environment -> container lifecycle
value.meaning: OCI Runtime Specification defines configuration, execution environment and lifecycle.

value.name: Container image structure

value.meaning: OCI Image Specification defines these image components.

value.name: Container cluster management
value.expression: Cluster management = create + upgrade + repair + balance + scale + log + monitor
value.meaning: Source lists these as cluster management functions.

value.name: Demand-responsive scaling
value.expression: User demand change -> start/stop instances -> adjusted capacity
value.meaning: Cluster management adapts capacity to number of users by starting or stopping instances.

value.name: Shared-kernel security boundary
value.expression: Shared OS kernel -> common attack surface -> possible system-wide impact
value.meaning: Source warns that shared OS architecture can allow security threats to affect the whole containerized system.

value.name: Container orchestration
value.expression: Application containers + orchestration controller -> coordinated container management
value.meaning: Orchestration is mainly used for application containers and includes Kubernetes and Docker Swarm.

value.name: Container vs Virtual Machine
value.description: Containerization uses OS/application-level virtualization and shared kernels; system VMs can provide whole-machine/guest-OS abstractions.

value.name: OS Container vs Application Container
value.description: Source identifies OS containers and application containers as distinct container types.

value.name: Container vs Container Image
value.description: Container is an execution environment; image is a packaged artifact whose structure is standardized by OCI.

value.name: Image vs Runtime
value.description: Image describes packaged filesystem/configuration content; runtime defines execution environment and lifecycle.

value.name: Runtime Specification vs Image Specification
value.description: Runtime Specification covers execution/lifecycle; Image Specification covers image structure.

value.name: OCI Distribution vs Image Specification
value.description: Distribution concerns image distribution; Image Specification concerns image representation.

value.name: Container Management vs Orchestration
value.description: Management encompasses operational functions; orchestration specifically coordinates application containers.

value.name: Orchestration vs Cluster Management
value.description: Orchestration coordinates application containers; cluster management covers infrastructure/cluster lifecycle, scaling and observability.

value.name: Shared Kernel vs Separate Guest OS
value.description: Containers share a kernel; system VMs provide guest OS execution.

value.name: Portability vs Interoperability
value.description: Portability concerns running across environments/vendors; interoperability concerns compatible implementations/tools under common standards.

value.name: OS Security Scanning vs Application Security
value.description: Protecting the host OS does not necessarily protect application containers.

value.name: Scaling vs Load Balancing
value.description: Scaling changes the number of instances; load balancing distributes load among existing instances.

value.name: Logging vs Monitoring
value.description: Logging records activities; monitoring observes logs, applications or sensors.

value.name: Container Runtime vs Container Manager
value.description: Runtime implements execution/lifecycle; manager/orchestrator manages groups/workloads.

value.name: Cloud vs Non-cloud Container Deployment
value.description: Containerization explicitly spans both cloud and non-cloud environments.

value.name: Container Security Benefit vs Security Risk
value.description: Isolation provides separation, but shared-kernel architecture creates a broader security concern.

value.name: Cluster Repair vs Upgrade
value.description: Repair restores operational state; upgrade changes software versions/state.

value.name: Application Dependency vs Kernel Dependency
value.description: Libraries/configuration/dependencies are bundled per application; containers still depend on a shared OS kernel.

value.misconception: Containers are just small virtual machines.
value.correction: The source frames containers as OS/application-level virtualization and emphasizes shared kernel operation.

value.misconception: Every container has its own operating-system kernel.
value.correction: Multiple containers collectively share a common OS kernel.

value.misconception: A container is the same thing as a container image.
value.correction: The image is the packaged artifact; the container is the execution environment.

value.misconception: OCI only standardizes container images.
value.correction: OCI maintains Runtime, Image and Distribution specifications.

value.misconception: OCI Runtime Specification defines image layers.
value.correction: Runtime Specification defines configuration/execution/lifecycle; image layers belong to Image Specification.

value.misconception: Orchestration and cluster management are identical.
value.correction: The source distinguishes application-container orchestration from broader cluster management functions.

value.misconception: Scaling just means load balancing.
value.correction: Scaling changes instance count; load balancing balances work among existing instances.

value.misconception: OS security scanning automatically secures application containers.
value.correction: The source explicitly warns that scanners generally protect the OS but may not protect application containers.

value.misconception: Containerization only applies to public cloud.
value.correction: The source explicitly includes non-cloud environments.

value.misconception: Containerization eliminates security risk through isolation.
value.correction: The shared OS can allow security threats to affect the whole containerized system.

value.misconception: Kubernetes is the only container orchestrator.
value.correction: The source names both Kubernetes and Docker Swarm and its taxonomy also lists OpenShift and Amazon ECS.

value.misconception: Container clusters only need scheduling.
value.correction: The source lists creation, upgrades, repair, balancing, scaling, logging and monitoring.

Containers surround applications, bundle configuration/libraries/dependencies, isolate processes, and collectively share an OS kernel.
Containerization is widely adopted by major cloud platforms and pursued by the U.S. Department of Defense, first applied to the F-22.

OCI develops Runtime, Image and Distribution specifications intended to provide interoperability.
Container orchestration/management is mainly used for application containers, with Kubernetes and Docker Swarm named as implementations.
Container cluster management includes creation, upgrade, repair, load balancing, scaling, logging and monitoring.
The source provides journal literature covering containerization technologies, applications, challenges and cloud distributed systems.
The source provides books on containerization and Docker.

semantic_distinctions.name: Logging vs Monitoring
semantic_distinctions.description: Logging records activities; monitoring observes logs, applications or sensors.

semantic_distinctions.name: Container Runtime vs Container Manager
semantic_distinctions.description: Runtime implements execution/lifecycle; manager/orchestrator manages groups/workloads.

semantic_distinctions.name: Cloud vs Non-cloud Container Deployment
semantic_distinctions.description: Containerization explicitly spans both cloud and non-cloud environments.

semantic_distinctions.name: Container Security Benefit vs Security Risk
semantic_distinctions.description: Isolation provides separation, but shared-kernel architecture creates a broader security concern.

semantic_distinctions.name: Cluster Repair vs Upgrade
semantic_distinctions.description: Repair restores operational state; upgrade changes software versions/state.

semantic_distinctions.name: Application Dependency vs Kernel Dependency
semantic_distinctions.description: Libraries/configuration/dependencies are bundled per application; containers still depend on a shared OS kernel.

misconceptions.misconception: Containers are just small virtual machines.
misconceptions.correction: The source frames containers as OS/application-level virtualization and emphasizes shared kernel operation.

misconceptions.misconception: Every container has its own operating-system kernel.
misconceptions.correction: Multiple containers collectively share a common OS kernel.

misconceptions.misconception: A container is the same thing as a container image.
misconceptions.correction: The image is the packaged artifact; the container is the execution environment.

misconceptions.misconception: OCI only standardizes container images.
misconceptions.correction: OCI maintains Runtime, Image and Distribution specifications.

misconceptions.misconception: OCI Runtime Specification defines image layers.
misconceptions.correction: Runtime Specification defines configuration/execution/lifecycle; image layers belong to Image Specification.

misconceptions.misconception: Orchestration and cluster management are identical.
misconceptions.correction: The source distinguishes application-container orchestration from broader cluster management functions.

misconceptions.misconception: Scaling just means load balancing.
misconceptions.correction: Scaling changes instance count; load balancing balances work among existing instances.

misconceptions.misconception: OS security scanning automatically secures application containers.
misconceptions.correction: The source explicitly warns that scanners generally protect the OS but may not protect application containers.

misconceptions.misconception: Containerization only applies to public cloud.
misconceptions.correction: The source explicitly includes non-cloud environments.

misconceptions.misconception: Containerization eliminates security risk through isolation.
misconceptions.correction: The shared OS can allow security threats to affect the whole containerized system.

misconceptions.misconception: Kubernetes is the only container orchestrator.
misconceptions.correction: The source names both Kubernetes and Docker Swarm and its taxonomy also lists OpenShift and Amazon ECS.

misconceptions.misconception: Container clusters only need scheduling.
misconceptions.correction: The source lists creation, upgrades, repair, balancing, scaling, logging and monitoring.

why_it_matters.core_problem: Package applications into isolated, portable environments while sharing operating-system resources and coordinating those environments at cluster scale.
why_it_matters.mechanism_chain: Application dependencies/configuration -> container artifact/runtime -> isolated process environment -> shared kernel -> orchestration -> cluster management -> scaling/observability.
why_it_matters.central_insight: Containerization is not merely packaging software. In the supplied source it is a layered system spanning virtualization boundaries, application packaging, standardized images/runtimes/distribution, orchestration and cluster operations, with a distinct shared-kernel security model.

source_claims.statement: C++ originated as an extension of C and evolved into a multi-paradigm language.
Stroustrup began C with Classes at Bell Labs in 1979.
C++ combines direct hardware mapping with zero-overhead abstractions.
C++ is standardized by ISO WG21 and has successive revisions.
The standard library spans containers, iterators, ranges, algorithms, numerics, I/O, memory, metaprogramming, diagnostics and concurrency.
The STL model of containers, iterators and generic algorithms became part of the standard library.
C++ is not strictly a superset of C.
extern C enables C linkage for mixed C/C++ functions.
Assembly integration varies by compiler and architecture.
Core Guidelines target type/resource safety but are not ISO consensus.
Manual memory misuse can introduce security risks such as buffer overflow.
C++ influenced a broad set of later languages.

value.title: C vs CUDA C/C++
value.description: C/C++ is the language base; CUDA adds GPU execution, memory and API extensions.

value.title: Host vs device
value.description: Host code runs on CPU; device kernels run on GPU.

value.title: Runtime API vs Driver API
value.description: Runtime is higher-level/single-source; Driver API is lower-level/non-single-source.

value.title: Grid vs block vs thread
value.description: Grid contains blocks; blocks contain threads; warps group 32 threads.

value.title: Shared vs global memory
value.description: Shared memory is block-shared/user-managed; global memory is device-wide.

value.title: PTX vs SASS
value.description: PTX is intermediate representation; SASS is hardware machine instruction representation.

value.title: CUDA vs ROCm
value.description: CUDA is proprietary NVIDIA software; ROCm is open-source AMD software.

value.title: CUDA vs oneAPI
value.description: CUDA is NVIDIA-specific; oneAPI targets multiple architectures through open specifications.

value.title: Uniform vs divergent warp control flow
value.description: Uniform branches preserve SIMD efficiency; divergence reduces it.

value.title: Computation vs transfer cost
value.description: Host/device transfers can limit end-to-end acceleration.

value.claim: CUDA is just C
value.correction: CUDA C/C++ adds GPU kernels, execution hierarchy, memory APIs and a CUDA compilation/runtime model.

value.claim: CUDA runs all code on the GPU
value.correction: Host code remains CPU-side while kernels execute on the GPU.

value.claim: A block is a GPU core
value.correction: A block is a logical group of threads scheduled onto streaming multiprocessors.

value.claim: A thread is a CUDA core
value.correction: Threads are logical execution contexts; hardware execution is organized through warps and SMs.

value.claim: PTX is final machine code
value.correction: PTX is an intermediate representation that is lowered toward GPU machine instructions.

value.claim: More threads always means faster
value.correction: Warp divergence, memory movement, architecture and occupancy constraints can dominate.

value.claim: Shared memory is VRAM
value.correction: Shared memory is a distinct fast user-managed region shared by block threads.

value.claim: CUDA runs natively on every GPU vendor
value.correction: CUDA is proprietary/NVIDIA-specific; compatibility and alternative stacks exist for other vendors.

value.name: Container execution model
value.expression: Container = isolated processes + packaged software/configuration + shared host kernel
value.meaning: Docker containers encapsulate application processes and dependencies while sharing the host operating-system kernel.

value.name: Image-to-container relation
value.expression: Image (read-only template) -> Container (runtime instance)
value.meaning: A Docker image stores the packaged application template used to build/run containers.

value.name: Linux resource control
value.expression: Container resource usage <= cgroup limits
value.meaning: cgroups provide resource limiting for CPU and memory.

value.name: Linux namespace isolation
value.expression: Container view = isolated(process tree, network, user IDs, mounts)
value.meaning: Namespaces isolate an application's view of key operating-environment resources.

value.name: Registry distribution flow
value.expression: Build -> Image -> push -> Registry -> pull -> Runtime
value.meaning: Images can be built, uploaded to a registry, then downloaded by clients for use.

value.name: Compose application flow
value.expression: Compose YAML -> Services -> Containers -> Multi-container application
value.meaning: Compose defines service configuration and creates/starts/scales containers.

value.name: Swarm consensus condition
value.expression: Commit update only if approvals > N/2
value.meaning: Source states Swarm uses Raft and a majority of nodes must agree for an update.

value.name: Container data persistence
value.expression: Volume lifetime > Container lifetime
value.meaning: Docker Volume allows data to survive deletion/recreation of a container.

equations.meaning: Compose defines service configuration and creates/starts/scales containers.

equations.name: Container data persistence

equations.meaning: Docker Volume allows data to survive deletion/recreation of a container.

source_claims.claim: Docker packages software in lightweight containers using OS-level virtualization and automates deployment across environments.
Docker originated as a dotCloud internal project, debuted publicly in 2013, used LXC initially, then moved to libcontainer and later created Moby.
Docker adoption expanded through Red Hat, Microsoft, AWS, IBM, Oracle, Windows/WSL2, Docker Desktop licensing, AtomicJar, and major 2025 releases.
Docker uses Linux kernel interfaces, namespaces, cgroups and union-capable filesystems; macOS uses a Linux VM.
Docker software architecture includes dockerd, Docker CLI, Docker objects, registries and Dockerfiles.
Dockerfile example uses ARG, FROM, COPY, ENV, RUN, VOLUME and EXPOSE.
Docker Compose defines/runs multi-container applications and Docker Swarm provides clustering and Raft consensus.
Docker Volumes provide independent persistence and licensing differs between Docker Engine and Docker Desktop.
Related technologies include Linux, DevOps, gVisor, Kubernetes, microservices, OCI and related software architecture.

historical_events.event: Docker began as an internal dotCloud project and debuted publicly at PyCon.
Docker 0.9 replaced LXC as default execution environment with libcontainer.
Docker created the Moby project for open research and development.
Docker Desktop licensing changed for larger enterprise users.
Docker acquired AtomicJar.
Docker Engine 28 hardened default container networking.
Docker Desktop 4.41 expanded Docker Model Runner.
Docker Engine 29 made containerd image store default for fresh installations.
VisualDock Server was released according to the source.

fields.label: Semantic distinctions
value: Kubernetes primarily represents desired state as objects; controllers determine corrective actions rather than requiring users to script every individual machine operation.
Control plane coordinates state; nodes execute workloads.
spec expresses desired state; status records current state.
Container is the runtime unit; Pod is the Kubernetes deployable unit that groups one or more containers.
Service provides stable identity/load balancing over a changing set of Pods.
ReplicaSet maintains replica count; Deployment manages ReplicaSets and rollout/rollback.
Stateful workloads require stable identity/order/persistence; stateless workloads generally scale by adding equivalent replicas.
Container filesystems can disappear on restart; volumes provide persistent/shared storage.
CRD defines an API type; Operator combines custom resources with controllers to automate domain-specific behavior.
Authentication establishes identity; authorization decides what that identity may do.
kubelet manages Pod state; runtime executes container lifecycle through CRI.
Pod IPs are tied to individual Pods; Service identity remains stable while matching Pods change.
Namespaces organize/partition resources; authorization determines permitted API actions.
CSI separates storage integration implementation from Kubernetes core.
Scheduler decides where an unscheduled Pod runs; controllers continuously reconcile resource state.
Desired state is declared intent; actual state is observed runtime condition.
Scaling changes capacity/replicas; resilience restores service after failures or drift.
Both externalize configuration, but Secret is intended for confidential data.

value.misconception: Kubernetes is a virtual machine hypervisor
value.correction: Kubernetes orchestrates workloads; it can run on virtual machines or bare metal but is not itself the VM hypervisor.

value.misconception: A Pod is just a container
value.correction: A Pod is the deployable unit and can contain one or more co-located containers.

value.misconception: A Service is a Pod with a stable IP
value.correction: A Service is an abstraction over a selected set of Pods and provides stable network identity.

value.misconception: Scheduler keeps desired replica counts
value.correction: Scheduler places unscheduled Pods; controllers reconcile resource state and replica counts.

value.misconception: etcd runs containers
value.correction: etcd stores cluster state; container runtime executes containers on nodes.

value.misconception: Secrets are automatically encrypted at rest
value.correction: The source explicitly notes Secrets are not encrypted at rest by default and require additional setup.

value.misconception: Namespace alone provides full security isolation
value.correction: Namespaces partition resources, while authorization controls API permissions.

value.misconception: StatefulSet itself is a database
value.correction: StatefulSet provides identity/order orchestration properties; the database remains the application.

value.misconception: kubelet decides cluster-wide placement
value.correction: kubelet maintains workload state on its node; scheduler selects nodes.

value.misconception: Reconciliation is a one-time deployment step
value.correction: Controllers continuously drive actual state toward desired state.

value.misconception: Pod IP is the stable application endpoint
value.correction: Pods can be replaced; Services provide stable IP/DNS identity.

value.misconception: CRD automatically runs the application
value.correction: CRD defines an API resource type; a controller/operator provides behavior.

value.core_problem: Coordinate desired software state across changing distributed compute infrastructure without requiring humans to manually orchestrate every machine and recovery action.

major_value_propositions.because: Controllers turn desired-state declarations into repeatable reconciliation loops.
Failure-induced divergence can trigger replacement/recovery actions.
Schedulers and workload controllers coordinate resource supply with workload demand.

source_claims.title: Definition
source_claims.claim: Kubernetes is an open-source container orchestration system for automating deployment, scaling, and management of containerized workloads.

source_claims.title: Cluster model
source_claims.claim: Kubernetes assembles virtual or bare-metal computers into a cluster capable of running container workloads.

source_claims.title: Control-plane/node architecture
source_claims.claim: Kubernetes separates management/control-plane components from worker nodes and exposes resources through an object/API model.

source_claims.title: etcd state store
source_claims.claim: etcd persistently represents cluster configuration/state and favors consistency during network partitions.

source_claims.title: API server
source_claims.claim: The API server exposes the Kubernetes API, validates REST requests, persists API-object state, and participates in watch-driven coordination.

source_claims.title: Scheduler
source_claims.claim: The scheduler matches unscheduled Pods to nodes using resource availability and constraints.

source_claims.title: Controllers
source_claims.claim: Controllers reconcile actual cluster state toward desired state and can replace failed workloads.

source_claims.title: kubelet
source_claims.claim: kubelet maintains Pod/container state on each node and reports node status.

source_claims.title: Runtime_CRi
source_claims.claim: The container runtime manages container lifecycle while CRI decouples kubelet from implementation.

source_claims.title: Networking
source_claims.claim: kube-proxy implements network proxy/load-balancing behavior for Services.

source_claims.title: Namespaces
source_claims.claim: Namespaces segregate Kubernetes resources across teams/projects/environments.

source_claims.title: Pods
source_claims.claim: Pods are the basic deployable unit and group one or more co-located containers with a Pod network identity.

source_claims.title: Workloads
source_claims.claim: Higher-level workload objects declaratively manage Pods, including ReplicaSets, Deployments, StatefulSets and DaemonSets.

source_claims.title: Services
source_claims.claim: Services provide stable IP/DNS identity and load-balance traffic to Pods selected by labels.

source_claims.title: Storage
source_claims.claim: Volumes, persistent storage, Container Attached Storage, and CSI address storage persistence and external storage integration.

source_claims.title: Configuration
source_claims.claim: ConfigMaps and Secrets externalize configuration; Secrets are intended for confidential data and require additional protection for at-rest encryption.

source_claims.title: API objects
source_claims.claim: Kubernetes objects record intent with metadata, spec, status, ownership, and lifecycle semantics.

source_claims.title: Extensions
source_claims.claim: CRDs, custom controllers, and Operators extend Kubernetes declaratively.

source_claims.title: API security
source_claims.claim: TLS, authentication, and authorization mechanisms protect the Kubernetes API.

source_claims.title: Cluster API
source_claims.claim: Cluster API applies Kubernetes object/API principles to infrastructure and machines.

source_claims.title: Uses
source_claims.claim: Kubernetes is used across deployment, scaling, cloud/data-center management, observability, and related infrastructure workflows.

source_claims.title: Complexity/criticism
source_claims.claim: The source discusses complexity, ecosystem fragmentation, operational difficulty, and reasons managed services/PaaS approaches emerged.

source_claims.title: History
source_claims.claim: Kubernetes originated at Google, drew on Borg and Promise Theory, was announced in 2014, and was contributed to CNCF.

source_claims.title: Release timeline
source_claims.claim: The source contains a release/support timeline through Kubernetes 1.36 and related support windows.

why_it_matters.core_problem: Coordinate desired software state across changing distributed compute infrastructure without requiring humans to manually orchestrate every machine and recovery action.

value.source_authority: Supplied article is authoritative for this transformation.
value.transformation_policy: Preserve concepts, mechanisms, purposes, examples, historical relationships, distinctions, references and source context. Do not silently correct or replace source claims.
value.core_thesis: An operating system is system software that manages computer hardware/software resources and provides common services, while mediating hardware access, isolating applications, abstracting hardware, scheduling execution, managing memory/I/O, and providing security and portability mechanisms.
value.relationship_policy: Relationships are directional and mechanism-bearing where possible. Rich edges preserve mechanism, effect, conditions, inverse/converse, scope and architectural context.

value.mechanism: The OS decides when applications receive CPU time and how much memory/resources they receive.
value.effect: Prevents a single application from monopolizing limited hardware and enables concurrent application execution.
value.conditions: Multiple applications contend for finite CPU and memory resources.
value.inverse_or_converse: Without allocation, one program could monopolize resources.

value.mechanism: The OS separates applications so errors and security vulnerabilities in one application are contained while communication remains possible.
value.effect: Improves reliability and security without eliminating application communication.
value.conditions: Isolation must coexist with controlled inter-application communication.
value.inverse_or_converse: Unrestricted sharing increases interference risk.

value.mechanism: OS interfaces hide hardware-access details such as physical memory behind standardized services/interfaces.
value.effect: Programmers can develop against OS abstractions rather than hardware-specific details.
value.conditions: Hardware differences remain beneath the abstraction.
value.inverse_or_converse: Bypassing abstractions increases hardware dependence.

value.mechanism: OS exposes reusable interfaces for networking, disks and other common facilities.
value.effect: Applications can run across different hardware without being rewritten for each hardware implementation.
value.conditions: Service set varies greatly between OS designs.
value.inverse_or_converse: Missing services can force applications to depend on hardware-specific implementations.

value.mechanism: Paging/segmentation let the kernel choose mappings and use disk/RAM as a larger logical memory space.
value.effect: A program can perceive a large continuous address space even when physical memory is scattered or limited.
value.conditions: Requires hardware support and OS memory-management mechanisms.
value.inverse_or_converse: Invalid/restricted addresses can trigger faults.

value.mechanism: Kernel-enforced protection separates applications/users and limits their resource authority.
value.effect: Errors remain isolated and malicious software has less power to compromise private data or monopolize resources.
value.conditions: Depends on hardware privilege/memory-protection mechanisms.
value.inverse_or_converse: Broken protection increases cross-process interference.

value.mechanism: Hardware checks user-mode software for legal instructions while kernel mode has unrestricted powers.
value.effect: Separates ordinary application execution from privileged OS control.
value.conditions: Requires processor support for privilege modes.
value.inverse_or_converse: Executing privileged operations from user mode is prevented or traps to the kernel.

value.mechanism: The kernel creates a process, assigns memory/resources/priority, loads its binary and starts execution.
value.effect: Turns an application program into a managed unit of execution.
value.conditions: Exact process model varies by OS.
value.inverse_or_converse: An application may also execute another application within the same process or via a separate thread in systems described.

value.mechanism: An interrupt changes CPU control flow to an interrupt service routine; state is saved and later restored.
value.effect: Allows the OS to react efficiently to hardware/software events.
value.conditions: Architecture-specific interrupt handling differs.
value.inverse_or_converse: No interrupt handling would prevent timely OS reaction to device/events.

value.mechanism: When a device completes I/O it can interrupt the running process/CPU and provide status information.
value.effect: The OS can resume or schedule the process associated with the completed I/O.
value.conditions: Uses interrupt handlers, process state and context switching.
value.inverse_or_converse: If completion is not handled, the waiting process cannot be resumed normally.

value.mechanism: The scheduler changes the running process by saving one process's CPU state and restoring another's.
value.effect: CPU time is shared among runnable processes.
value.conditions: Depends on saved CPU state such as registers and program counter.
value.inverse_or_converse: A context switch is unnecessary when no process change occurs.

value.mechanism: Hardware-supported segmentation or paging restricts which addresses a process may access.
value.effect: One process cannot normally overwrite another process's memory; invalid access triggers an interrupt/fault.
value.conditions: Requires hardware support such as an MMU.
value.inverse_or_converse: A faulty/malicious access can cause a segmentation violation and process termination.

value.mechanism: Protected registers define permitted address regions; invalid access causes an interrupt and re-entry into supervisor mode.
value.effect: The kernel regains control and can terminate the offending program.
value.conditions: The source describes segmentation violation as a common response.
value.inverse_or_converse: Valid access avoids the fault.

value.mechanism: When one job waits for I/O, another job can use the CPU; multiple jobs are held in memory with partitioning and safeguards.
value.effect: Improves CPU utilization while preventing one job from accessing another's memory.
value.conditions: Requires memory partitioning/protection.
value.inverse_or_converse: Without multiprogramming, I/O wait would leave CPU less utilized.

value.mechanism: IEEE POSIX standardizes OS application-programming interfaces supported by most UNIX systems.
value.effect: Applications gain a common API target across compatible UNIX systems.
value.conditions: POSIX is an API compatibility standard, not an operating system.
value.inverse_or_converse: Nonstandard APIs reduce portability.

value.mechanism: OS services are provided as libraries and composed with one application/configuration code into a specialized single-address-space image.
value.effect: Avoids usual context-switch overhead and can deploy a minimal machine image.
value.conditions: Single application means traditional inter-application protection domains are unnecessary in the described model.
value.inverse_or_converse: More conventional OS boundaries reintroduce mode/context-switch overhead.

value.mechanism: Mode switching can pollute important processor structures including caches and the instruction pipeline.
value.effect: System-call/mode-switch overhead can reduce user- and kernel-mode performance beyond direct switching cost.
value.conditions: The cited FlexSC discussion emphasizes both direct and indirect costs.
value.inverse_or_converse: Avoiding or reducing mode switches can reduce this source of overhead.

value.mechanism: Remote direct memory access permits one CPU to access memory belonging to another CPU.
value.effect: Reduces reliance on packet copying for cross-CPU data movement.
value.conditions: Architecture/network support is required.
value.inverse_or_converse: Without RDMA, explicit communication/copying mechanisms are used.

value.mechanism: Middleware sits between OS and applications and is used to improve consistency across distinct networked computers.
value.effect: Provides a higher-level coordination layer without becoming the OS.
value.conditions: Each participating computer can retain its own OS and filesystem.
value.inverse_or_converse: Middleware is not itself a true OS.

value.mechanism: Hard real-time systems require exact processing by or at specified moments.
value.effect: Missed deadlines are unacceptable in the intended timing model.
value.conditions: Common in manufacturing, avionics and military uses per source.
value.inverse_or_converse: Soft real-time permits occasional missed events.

value.mechanism: Soft real-time accepts occasional missed events.
value.effect: Supports workloads such as audio/multimedia and smartphones where occasional deadline misses are acceptable.
value.conditions: Timing guarantee is weaker than hard real-time.
value.inverse_or_converse: Hard real-time does not permit the same relaxation.

value.mechanism: Windows uses ACLs, integrity levels, process authentication tokens and object security descriptors.
value.effect: Controls access to objects and processes and strengthens OS security.
value.conditions: Later releases add further security features.
value.inverse_or_converse: Removing access controls broadens authority.

value.mechanism: Android is closely based on Linux and uses a Linux kernel with Bionic.
value.effect: Provides a Linux-derived OS foundation for mobile and embedded systems.
value.conditions: Much Android code is written in Java and uses object-oriented design.
value.inverse_or_converse: The Android user-space stack differs from a conventional Linux distribution.

value.mechanism: Linux is written in C according to the source.
value.effect: Provides a low-level systems implementation foundation.
value.conditions: The source also describes UNIX-compatible syntax/networking and multiple-user preemptive multitasking.
value.inverse_or_converse: Different language choices would change implementation properties but not the OS abstraction itself.

value.mechanism: VMs can be paused, saved and resumed and can emulate hardware for an OS.
value.effect: Useful for OS research, development and debugging, while improving portability.
value.conditions: The VM acts as an application emulating hardware.
value.inverse_or_converse: Without virtualization, incompatible applications may require compatible base OS/hardware.

value.mechanism: Embedded systems described do not load user-installed software, so they may not need protection between applications.
value.effect: Permits very small/simple OS designs.
value.conditions: Applies to the embedded systems described in the source.
value.inverse_or_converse: General-purpose user-installed software would create stronger isolation requirements.

value.name: Resource allocation
value.expression: finite_resource -> scheduler/allocation -> application_share
value.meaning: OS divides scarce CPU time and memory/resource space among applications.

value.name: Program execution
value.expression: program -> kernel -> process -> memory/resources/priority -> binary_loaded -> execution
value.meaning: Typical application launch path described by the source.

value.name: Interrupt flow
value.expression: event -> interrupt -> ISR -> save_state -> service -> restore_state
value.meaning: Common hardware/software interrupt control-flow sequence.

value.name: Context switch
value.expression: old_process_state -> save -> new_process_state -> restore -> resume
value.meaning: CPU changes from one process to another.

value.name: Memory protection
value.expression: virtual_address -> paging/segmentation -> allowed_region | fault -> kernel
value.meaning: Hardware-supported protection restricts process memory access.

value.name: Virtual memory
value.expression: RAM + backing_store -> virtual_address_space -> process
value.meaning: Kernel presents memory as a logical address space larger/different from physical layout.

value.name: Linux system structure
value.expression: kernel + system_libraries + system_utilities -> Linux_distribution
value.meaning: Structure explicitly described for Linux distributions.

value.name: Library OS / unikernel
value.expression: libraries + application + configuration -> single_address_space_machine_image
value.meaning: Specialized machine image with only necessary library code.

value.name: Multicomputer communication
value.expression: CPU_A <-> messages/RDMA/RPC/DSM <-> CPU_B
value.meaning: Communication techniques listed for multicomputers.

value.name: POSIX portability
value.expression: UNIX_application -> POSIX_API -> compatible_UNIX_systems
value.meaning: POSIX improves compatibility among UNIX systems.

value.name: Windows security object model
value.expression: process -> authentication_token; object -> security_descriptor/ACL/integrity_level
value.meaning: Security mechanisms described for Windows.

value.name: Real-time timing
value.expression: event/data -> deadline -> hard_exact | soft_occasional_miss
value.meaning: Distinguishes hard and soft real-time behavior.

OS vs kernel
value.description: Kernel is the always-running core; an OS can include system programs and other software beyond the kernel.

value.label: OS vs application
value.description: OS provides resource management/services; applications are other software running on the computer.

value.label: OS abstraction vs direct hardware execution
value.description: Application code generally executes directly on hardware but requests OS services and follows OS rules for privileged/hardware operations.

value.label: Multiprocessor vs multicomputer
value.description: Multiprocessors share memory; multicomputers have multiple CPUs with separate memory.

value.label: Multicomputer vs distributed system
value.description: Multicomputers are tightly coupled CPU/memory systems; distributed systems are distinct networked computers potentially dispersed worldwide.

value.label: Middleware vs OS
value.description: Middleware can function similarly to an OS but is an additional layer and not a true OS.

value.label: Embedded vs general purpose
value.description: Embedded systems may omit user-application protection because they do not load user-installed software.

value.label: Hard vs soft real-time
value.description: Hard real-time requires exact timing; soft real-time tolerates occasional missed events.

value.label: Hypervisor vs VM
value.description: The source describes the hypervisor as running a VM, while the VM is the application that emulates hardware.

value.label: Library OS vs conventional OS
value.description: libOS provides OS services as libraries composed with an application, reducing protection/context-switch overhead in the described single-application model.

value.label: User mode vs kernel mode
value.description: User mode is hardware-restricted; kernel mode has unrestricted OS privilege.

value.label: Hardware vs software interrupt
value.description: Hardware interrupt reports an event to the CPU; software interrupt communicates an event to a process/change of execution.

value.label: Interrupt vs signal
value.description: Signals are Unix-like process notifications analogous to software/hardware interrupt behavior but are an OS process communication mechanism.

value.label: Segmentation vs paging
value.description: Both provide memory protection, but they are distinct address-management mechanisms requiring hardware support.

value.label: Virtual memory vs physical memory
value.description: Virtual memory presents a logical address space whose backing can span RAM and disk rather than exposing physical layout directly.

value.label: Context switch vs interrupt
value.description: An interrupt can cause a context switch, but an interrupt is the event/control-transfer mechanism whereas a context switch changes the running process.

value.label: Resource allocation vs isolation
value.description: Allocation shares finite resources; isolation prevents one application's errors/authority from interfering with others.

value.label: Portability vs abstraction
value.description: Hardware abstraction and common OS services let applications run across different hardware without rewriting hardware-specific access.

value.label: UNIX vs POSIX
value.description: UNIX is an OS family/history; POSIX is an API standard for compatibility.

value.label: Linux vs Android
value.description: Android is closely based on Linux but uses a distinct user-space stack including Bionic and substantial Java code.

value.label: GUI vs CLI
value.description: GUI provides graphical interaction; CLI is text-based command interaction.

value.label: Preemptive vs cooperative behavior
value.description: Preemptive multitasking lets the OS scheduler interrupt/reassign CPU execution rather than relying entirely on voluntary cooperation.

value.label: System call vs library call
value.description: System calls request kernel services; libOS services can be accessed through simple library calls without usual context switches.

value.label: Protection vs no protection
value.description: Some specialized OS designs deliberately omit conventional application protection when their workload model makes it unnecessary.

value.statement: An operating system is just the kernel.
value.correction: The source explicitly distinguishes the kernel from system programs and applications; an OS can include software beyond the kernel.

value.statement: Applications never execute directly on hardware.
value.correction: The source says application code is usually executed directly by hardware while interacting with OS services through calls/interrupts.

value.statement: OS abstraction means hardware is irrelevant.
value.correction: The OS abstracts hardware details, but the kernel, drivers and hardware privilege mechanisms still mediate execution.

value.statement: Multicomputer and multiprocessor mean the same thing.
value.correction: Multiprocessors share memory; multicomputers have separate memory per CPU.

value.statement: A distributed system is one giant computer.
value.correction: The source describes distinct networked computers, potentially dispersed worldwide, each with its own OS/filesystem.

value.statement: All operating systems require full application isolation.
value.correction: Embedded and some hard-real-time/library OS designs may omit protection between applications under their workload assumptions.

value.statement: Real-time means merely fast.
value.correction: Real-time is defined by timing guarantees/deadlines; hard real-time requires exact timing, not simply high throughput.

value.statement: A VM is the same thing as a hypervisor.
value.correction: The source distinguishes the hypervisor from the VM it runs.

value.statement: Virtual memory is the same as physical RAM.
value.correction: Virtual memory abstracts physical memory and can use scattered RAM and disk/backing storage.

value.statement: Every interrupt is a context switch.
value.correction: An interrupt can cause a context switch; the interrupt itself is the event/control-transfer mechanism.

value.statement: A software interrupt is a hardware interrupt.
value.correction: The source distinguishes software interrupts/messages to processes from hardware interrupts/messages to the CPU.

value.statement: POSIX is a UNIX operating system.
value.correction: POSIX is an API standard intended to increase compatibility among UNIX systems.

rich_semantic_relationships.mechanism: Middleware sits between OS and applications and is used to improve consistency across distinct networked computers.
rich_semantic_relationships.effect: Provides a higher-level coordination layer without becoming the OS.
rich_semantic_relationships.conditions: Each participating computer can retain its own OS and filesystem.
rich_semantic_relationships.inverse_or_converse: Middleware is not itself a true OS.

rich_semantic_relationships.mechanism: Hard real-time systems require exact processing by or at specified moments.
rich_semantic_relationships.effect: Missed deadlines are unacceptable in the intended timing model.
rich_semantic_relationships.conditions: Common in manufacturing, avionics and military uses per source.
rich_semantic_relationships.inverse_or_converse: Soft real-time permits occasional missed events.

rich_semantic_relationships.mechanism: Soft real-time accepts occasional missed events.
rich_semantic_relationships.effect: Supports workloads such as audio/multimedia and smartphones where occasional deadline misses are acceptable.
rich_semantic_relationships.conditions: Timing guarantee is weaker than hard real-time.
rich_semantic_relationships.inverse_or_converse: Hard real-time does not permit the same relaxation.

rich_semantic_relationships.mechanism: Windows uses ACLs, integrity levels, process authentication tokens and object security descriptors.
rich_semantic_relationships.effect: Controls access to objects and processes and strengthens OS security.
rich_semantic_relationships.conditions: Later releases add further security features.
rich_semantic_relationships.inverse_or_converse: Removing access controls broadens authority.

rich_semantic_relationships.mechanism: Android is closely based on Linux and uses a Linux kernel with Bionic.
rich_semantic_relationships.effect: Provides a Linux-derived OS foundation for mobile and embedded systems.
rich_semantic_relationships.conditions: Much Android code is written in Java and uses object-oriented design.
rich_semantic_relationships.inverse_or_converse: The Android user-space stack differs from a conventional Linux distribution.

rich_semantic_relationships.mechanism: Linux is written in C according to the source.
rich_semantic_relationships.effect: Provides a low-level systems implementation foundation.
rich_semantic_relationships.conditions: The source also describes UNIX-compatible syntax/networking and multiple-user preemptive multitasking.
rich_semantic_relationships.inverse_or_converse: Different language choices would change implementation properties but not the OS abstraction itself.

rich_semantic_relationships.mechanism: VMs can be paused, saved and resumed and can emulate hardware for an OS.
rich_semantic_relationships.effect: Useful for OS research, development and debugging, while improving portability.
rich_semantic_relationships.conditions: The VM acts as an application emulating hardware.
rich_semantic_relationships.inverse_or_converse: Without virtualization, incompatible applications may require compatible base OS/hardware.

rich_semantic_relationships.mechanism: Embedded systems described do not load user-installed software, so they may not need protection between applications.
rich_semantic_relationships.effect: Permits very small/simple OS designs.
rich_semantic_relationships.conditions: Applies to the embedded systems described in the source.
rich_semantic_relationships.inverse_or_converse: General-purpose user-installed software would create stronger isolation requirements.

source_claims.statement: An operating system manages computer hardware/software resources and provides common services for computer programs.
Time-sharing OSes schedule tasks for efficient system use and may account for resource consumption.
OS acts as an intermediary for input/output and memory allocation while application code usually executes directly on hardware.
OS resource allocation shares CPU time/memory and prevents one program monopolizing limited hardware.
OS isolates applications to protect against errors/security vulnerabilities while enabling communication.
OS abstracts hardware access and virtualization can mask limited hardware resources.
OS common services for network/disk access enable applications to run across different hardware.
Multicomputers have multiple CPUs with separate memory and need efficient communication.
Distributed systems consist of distinct networked computers that may have their own OS/filesystem; middleware can improve consistency.
Embedded OSes target embedded systems and may omit application protection when no user-installed software is loaded.
Hard real-time systems require exact timing; soft real-time permits occasional missed events.
Hypervisors run VMs that emulate hardware and support OS research/development/debugging and portability.
Library OS services can be composed into a specialized single-address-space unikernel.
Early computers were directly programmed without OSes; operators manually performed scheduling/resource-management tasks.
OS/360 popularized multiprogramming and required memory partitioning and safeguards.
MULTICS targeted hundreds of simultaneous users; UNIX originated as a single-user development of MULTICS.
UNIX source availability led to System V and BSD; POSIX improved compatibility.
MINIX inspired Linux; MINIX later appeared in Intel microchip controllers.
CP/M was popular on early microcomputers; MS-DOS/IBM PC DOS became widespread on IBM PC compatibles.
Macintosh popularized GUI; Windows evolved from a GUI overlay to standalone Windows NT.
Android became a major mobile OS, using a Linux kernel and Bionic C library.
Kernel protects applications/users, manages memory, controls I/O, and separates user/kernel privilege.
Program execution typically creates a process, assigns resources/priority, loads binary code and starts execution.
Interrupts transfer control to an ISR and require saving/restoring execution state.
Software interrupts can represent normal timing, errors, user messages, and process communication.
Unix signals communicate asynchronous events; pipes coordinate producer/consumer processes.
Memory protection uses hardware-supported segmentation/paging; invalid access can trigger a segmentation violation.
Virtual memory can map scattered RAM/disk storage into a logical continuous address space.
Windows uses NTFS, Windows Driver Model, demand paging, preemptive scheduling, ACLs, integrity levels, authentication tokens and security descriptors.
Linux is distributed under GPL, uses a kernel/libraries/utilities structure, supports UNIX networking and preemptive multitasking, and can operate from small systems to large multiprocessors.

semantic_distinctions.label: OS vs kernel
semantic_distinctions.description: Kernel is the always-running core; an OS can include system programs and other software beyond the kernel.

semantic_distinctions.label: OS vs application
semantic_distinctions.description: OS provides resource management/services; applications are other software running on the computer.

semantic_distinctions.label: OS abstraction vs direct hardware execution
semantic_distinctions.description: Application code generally executes directly on hardware but requests OS services and follows OS rules for privileged/hardware operations.

semantic_distinctions.label: Multiprocessor vs multicomputer
semantic_distinctions.description: Multiprocessors share memory; multicomputers have multiple CPUs with separate memory.

semantic_distinctions.label: Multicomputer vs distributed system
semantic_distinctions.description: Multicomputers are tightly coupled CPU/memory systems; distributed systems are distinct networked computers potentially dispersed worldwide.

semantic_distinctions.label: Middleware vs OS
semantic_distinctions.description: Middleware can function similarly to an OS but is an additional layer and not a true OS.

semantic_distinctions.label: Embedded vs general purpose
semantic_distinctions.description: Embedded systems may omit user-application protection because they do not load user-installed software.

semantic_distinctions.label: Hard vs soft real-time
semantic_distinctions.description: Hard real-time requires exact timing; soft real-time tolerates occasional missed events.

semantic_distinctions.label: Hypervisor vs VM
semantic_distinctions.description: The source describes the hypervisor as running a VM, while the VM is the application that emulates hardware.

semantic_distinctions.label: Library OS vs conventional OS
semantic_distinctions.description: libOS provides OS services as libraries composed with an application, reducing protection/context-switch overhead in the described single-application model.

semantic_distinctions.label: User mode vs kernel mode
semantic_distinctions.description: User mode is hardware-restricted; kernel mode has unrestricted OS privilege.

semantic_distinctions.label: Hardware vs software interrupt
semantic_distinctions.description: Hardware interrupt reports an event to the CPU; software interrupt communicates an event to a process/change of execution.

semantic_distinctions.label: Interrupt vs signal
semantic_distinctions.description: Signals are Unix-like process notifications analogous to software/hardware interrupt behavior but are an OS process communication mechanism.

semantic_distinctions.label: Segmentation vs paging
semantic_distinctions.description: Both provide memory protection, but they are distinct address-management mechanisms requiring hardware support.

semantic_distinctions.label: Virtual memory vs physical memory
semantic_distinctions.description: Virtual memory presents a logical address space whose backing can span RAM and disk rather than exposing physical layout directly.

semantic_distinctions.label: Context switch vs interrupt
semantic_distinctions.description: An interrupt can cause a context switch, but an interrupt is the event/control-transfer mechanism whereas a context switch changes the running process.

semantic_distinctions.label: Resource allocation vs isolation
semantic_distinctions.description: Allocation shares finite resources; isolation prevents one application's errors/authority from interfering with others.

semantic_distinctions.label: Portability vs abstraction
semantic_distinctions.description: Hardware abstraction and common OS services let applications run across different hardware without rewriting hardware-specific access.

semantic_distinctions.label: UNIX vs POSIX
semantic_distinctions.description: UNIX is an OS family/history; POSIX is an API standard for compatibility.

semantic_distinctions.label: Linux vs Android
semantic_distinctions.description: Android is closely based on Linux but uses a distinct user-space stack including Bionic and substantial Java code.

semantic_distinctions.label: GUI vs CLI
semantic_distinctions.description: GUI provides graphical interaction; CLI is text-based command interaction.

semantic_distinctions.label: Preemptive vs cooperative behavior
semantic_distinctions.description: Preemptive multitasking lets the OS scheduler interrupt/reassign CPU execution rather than relying entirely on voluntary cooperation.

semantic_distinctions.label: System call vs library call
semantic_distinctions.description: System calls request kernel services; libOS services can be accessed through simple library calls without usual context switches.

semantic_distinctions.label: Protection vs no protection
semantic_distinctions.description: Some specialized OS designs deliberately omit conventional application protection when their workload model makes it unnecessary.

misconceptions.statement: An operating system is just the kernel.
misconceptions.correction: The source explicitly distinguishes the kernel from system programs and applications; an OS can include software beyond the kernel.

misconceptions.statement: Applications never execute directly on hardware.
misconceptions.correction: The source says application code is usually executed directly by hardware while interacting with OS services through calls/interrupts.

misconceptions.statement: OS abstraction means hardware is irrelevant.
misconceptions.correction: The OS abstracts hardware details, but the kernel, drivers and hardware privilege mechanisms still mediate execution.

misconceptions.statement: Multicomputer and multiprocessor mean the same thing.
misconceptions.correction: Multiprocessors share memory; multicomputers have separate memory per CPU.

misconceptions.statement: A distributed system is one giant computer.
misconceptions.correction: The source describes distinct networked computers, potentially dispersed worldwide, each with its own OS/filesystem.

misconceptions.statement: All operating systems require full application isolation.
misconceptions.correction: Embedded and some hard-real-time/library OS designs may omit protection between applications under their workload assumptions.

misconceptions.statement: Real-time means merely fast.
misconceptions.correction: Real-time is defined by timing guarantees/deadlines; hard real-time requires exact timing, not simply high throughput.

misconceptions.statement: A VM is the same thing as a hypervisor.
misconceptions.correction: The source distinguishes the hypervisor from the VM it runs.

misconceptions.statement: Virtual memory is the same as physical RAM.
misconceptions.correction: Virtual memory abstracts physical memory and can use scattered RAM and disk/backing storage.

misconceptions.statement: Every interrupt is a context switch.
misconceptions.correction: An interrupt can cause a context switch; the interrupt itself is the event/control-transfer mechanism.

misconceptions.statement: A software interrupt is a hardware interrupt.
misconceptions.correction: The source distinguishes software interrupts/messages to processes from hardware interrupts/messages to the CPU.

misconceptions.statement: POSIX is a UNIX operating system.
misconceptions.correction: POSIX is an API standard intended to increase compatibility among UNIX systems.

source_claims.text: Optical disc image is a sector-by-sector disk image containing disc filesystem and data.
Images can be created from optical discs, file collections, or other image files.
ISO stores user data, not control headers/error correction; logical data sectors are 2,048 bytes.
An image can be transferred over data links/removable media unlike a physical optical disc.
Suitable driver software can expose ISO to the OS as though it were a physical optical disc.
ISO has no physical track concept and cannot fully represent multi-track discs.
Audio CDs cannot be represented as ISO because audio tracks contain continuous encoded audio rather than filesystems.
CUE/BIN, CCD/IMG, and MDS/MDF can store complete multi-track images with companion track metadata.
Historically, writing ISO to flash drives was limited by software tooling; raw-image writers later existed.
ISO is used for emulation, virtual CD-ROMs for hypervisors, and OS installation media.

source_claims.title: Identity and design
source_claims.statement: Python is high-level, general-purpose, multi-paradigm, readability-oriented, indentation-based, standard-library-rich and garbage-collected.

source_claims.title: Origin
source_claims.statement: Python was conceived by Guido van Rossum at CWI as a successor to ABC; implementation began in 1989 and first release was 0.9.0 in 1991.

source_claims.title: Governance
source_claims.statement: Guido left the BDFL role in 2018 and a five-member Steering Council was elected in 2019.

source_claims.title: Version history
source_claims.statement: Python 2.0 added major features; Python 3.0 was a major non-fully-compatible revision; typing capabilities began in Python 3.5.

source_claims.title: Philosophy
source_claims.statement: The Zen of Python emphasizes explicitness, simplicity, readability and practical consistency, while remaining a guideline.

source_claims.title: PEPs
source_claims.statement: PEPs document information, processes, naming and language proposals and are overseen by the Steering Council.

source_claims.title: Syntax
source_claims.statement: Python uses significant indentation and provides statements for assignment, control flow, exceptions, classes, functions, context management, imports, matching and generators.

source_claims.title: Expressions and semantics
source_claims.statement: Python distinguishes expressions and statements and supports comprehensions, lambdas, slicing, unpacking, string forms and dynamic references.

source_claims.title: Typing
source_claims.statement: Python uses duck typing with typed objects and untyped names while remaining strongly typed; annotations may be checked externally.

source_claims.title: Built-in types
source_claims.statement: Python provides bool, bytearray, bytes, complex, dict, float, frozenset, int, list, NoneType, range, set, str and tuple.

source_claims.title: Numeric semantics
source_claims.statement: Python supports true/floor division, modulo, exponentiation, matrix multiplication, arbitrary precision integers, Decimal and Fraction.

source_claims.title: Libraries
source_claims.statement: The standard library covers Internet protocols/formats, GUI, relational databases, pseudorandom numbers, decimals, regex and unit testing.

source_claims.title: Environments
source_claims.statement: Python implementations commonly provide REPLs; CPython includes IDLE and the ecosystem includes IPython, Jupyter and desktop/web IDEs.

source_claims.title: CPython
source_claims.statement: CPython is the reference implementation, written in C, compiling Python to bytecode executed by a VM.

source_claims.title: Alternative implementations
source_claims.statement: The source describes PyPy, Codon, MicroPython, CircuitPython, Pyston, Cinder, RustPython and Stackless Python.

source_claims.title: Compilers and transpilers
source_claims.statement: The ecosystem includes Brython, Transcrypt, Cython, PyJL, Nuitka, Numba, Pythran, RPython and MyHDL.

source_claims.title: Performance
source_claims.statement: JIT, static compilation, multiprocessing, efficient data structures and native numerical libraries can improve performance.

source_claims.title: Development lifecycle
source_claims.statement: Python development uses PEPs, community review, GitHub and a release process with incompatible, feature and bug-fix releases.

source_claims.title: Culture and influence
source_claims.statement: PyCon, Monty Python naming/culture, Pythonic terminology and the influence graph are described.

value.title: Sandbox (computer security) — Full Relationship-Rich Semantic Knowledge Graph
value.source_authority: The supplied source is authoritative for this transformation.
value.transformation_policy: Preserve source terminology, mechanisms, implementations, use cases, references and distinctions; no outside corrections or silent reconciliation.
value.core_thesis: A sandbox separates running programs inside a restricted environment and controls their available resources and host access to contain failures and vulnerabilities.
value.relationship_semantics: Directed relationships preserve mechanism, effect, conditions, scope, implementation, containment, restriction, comparison, use, historical association and provenance.

value.mechanism: Execution occurs inside a restricted environment with controlled resources and host-facing operations.
value.effect: Reduces the ability of failures and vulnerabilities to spread.
value.conditions: Strength depends on enforcement of the sandbox boundary.
value.inverse_or_converse: Broader host access weakens separation.

value.mechanism: Network, host inspection, input devices and other resources are disallowed or heavily restricted.
value.effect: Limits the guest's ability to harm the host.
value.conditions: Requires effective resource/access enforcement.
value.inverse_or_converse: Unrestricted host access weakens containment.

value.mechanism: System-call filtering is one of the Linux kernel mechanisms used for application sandboxing.
value.effect: Reduces the kernel interface exposed to a sandboxed application.
value.conditions: The source explicitly combines it with cgroups and namespaces.
value.inverse_or_converse: A broader syscall surface increases available operations.

value.mechanism: cgroups are a Linux kernel feature used as part of application sandboxing.
value.effect: Contributes resource control.
value.conditions: Source does not specify a complete cgroup policy.
value.inverse_or_converse: Broader resource allowance weakens containment.

value.mechanism: Linux namespaces are a kernel feature used as part of application sandboxing.
value.effect: Contributes process/environment separation.
value.conditions: Used with seccomp and cgroups.
value.inverse_or_converse: Broader namespace visibility weakens isolation.

value.mechanism: Each application receives its own Linux user ID.
value.effect: Creates application-level OS identity separation.
value.conditions: Mechanism stated directly by source.
value.inverse_or_converse: Shared identity would broaden permissions.

value.mechanism: Adds hardening to Android app sandboxing and permits sandboxing every app as described.
value.effect: Increases sandbox scope/hardening.
value.conditions: Source contrasts this with stock Android.

value.mechanism: A virtual machine emulates a complete host computer so a conventional guest OS can boot and run.
value.effect: Guest execution is separated from native host execution.
value.conditions: Host-resource access is mediated through the emulator.
value.inverse_or_converse: Direct native host access bypasses the described mediation.

value.mechanism: Host resources are accessed through the emulator rather than natively.
value.effect: Creates a mediated host/guest boundary.
value.conditions: Depends on the emulator/VM layer.
value.inverse_or_converse: Direct access bypasses mediation.

value.mechanism: Network-access restrictions and a restricted filesystem namespace define the jail boundary.
value.effect: Limits network and filesystem reach.
value.conditions: Source notes common use in virtual hosting.
value.inverse_or_converse: Removing restrictions expands reach.

value.mechanism: Predetermined rules govern process spawning, code injection, network use and file/registry access.
value.effect: Programs receive constrained access levels.
value.conditions: SELinux and AppArmor are cited implementations.
value.inverse_or_converse: More permissive rules increase authority.

value.mechanism: A sandbox mimics or replicates a target desktop and contains malware execution.
value.effect: Researchers can evaluate malware behavior without exposing the real target host.
value.conditions: A nonrepresentative environment may not reproduce target behavior.

source_claims.statement: Sandbox separates running programs to mitigate spread of system failures and software vulnerabilities.
Sandbox resources include storage and memory scratch space; network access, host inspection and input-device access are usually restricted.
Sandboxing can be comparable to virtualization when providing a highly controlled environment.
Sandboxing is implemented by executing software in a restricted operating-system environment.
Linux application sandboxing uses seccomp, cgroups and namespaces.
Android assigns each application its own Linux user ID for application sandboxing.
GrapheneOS hardens app sandboxing and allows sandboxing every app as described.
Apple App Sandbox is required for specified App Store apps and recommended for other signed apps.
Virtual machines emulate a complete host computer and mediate host-resource access through the emulator.
Jails restrict network access and filesystem namespace and are common in virtual hosting.
Rule-based execution controls process spawning, code injection, network access and file/registry operations.
Security researchers use sandboxing to analyze malware behavior in replicated target environments.
Google Native Client sandboxes compiled C/C++ code in browsers independently of the user's OS.
Capability systems use opaque tokens to grant specific rights and can operate at kernel or user-space levels.
Strict seccomp permits only read, write, exit and sigreturn.
HTML5 iframe sandboxing restricts embedded content.
Java virtual machines sandbox untrusted applets/code.
.NET CLR Code Access Security restricts untrusted code.
SFI isolates store, read and jump assembly instructions into memory segments.
Online judges and executable pastebins are sandbox use cases.

source_claims.claim: A VM virtualizes or emulates a computer system; system VMs execute whole OSs while process VMs execute programs in platform-independent environments.
System VM architecture includes host/guest terminology, historical time-sharing motivations, memory sharing, embedded uses, sandboxing and server consolidation.
Process VMs are host applications supporting one process and provide platform-independent programming environments; cluster-oriented variants abstract communication.
VM history spans 1960s time-sharing, IBM systems, compiler intermediate representations, p-code, Smalltalk, JIT, Self, HotSpot and register-based VMs.
Full virtualization and hardware-assisted virtualization are distinct techniques with IBM, Intel and AMD historical milestones and many implementation examples.
OS-level virtualization partitions resources through the kernel, shares the host OS kernel and includes Docker and container technologies.
Snapshots capture VM state/storage; overlays form a coherent virtual disk; migration moves VM state; failover uses last-known coherent backup state.
Nested virtualization recursively runs hypervisors/VMs and may rely on hardware support such as VMCS shadowing.
VMs are used for security isolation and compartmentalization architectures can limit malware spread.

source_claims.title: Definition
source_claims.statement: A volume or logical drive is a distinctly-addressable storage area with a single file system.

source_claims.title: Storage topology
source_claims.statement: Mass storage is commonly divided into partitions used as volumes; volumes may span multiple media for redundancy, while simple volumes use one medium without redundancy or striping.

source_claims.title: Windows example
source_claims.statement: The source's two-drive example maps D0/P0 to NTFS C:, D0/P1 to FAT32 D:, and D1/P0 to FAT32 E:.

source_claims.title: Partition versus volume recognition
source_claims.statement: An OS may recognize a partition without recognizing its volume when it is unformatted or uses an unsupported filesystem such as ext4 in the Windows example.

source_claims.title: File-packed volume
source_claims.statement: A volume can be packed in one file, such as an ISO9660 disc image or Apple Disk Image; because it is a file inside a host volume, it is not a partition.

source_claims.title: Windows mounting
source_claims.statement: Windows handles volumes in the kernel and configures volumes/mount points through Disk Management or diskpart; mounted volumes receive paths via drive letters or NTFS mount points.

source_claims.title: Unix mounting
source_claims.statement: Unix-like systems commonly use volume managers and mount; non-boot volumes are grafted into the filesystem tree at a mount point.

source_claims.title: Cross-volume performance
source_claims.statement: Moving a file within a volume can change metadata without copying content, while moving across volumes requires copying content and deleting the source.

source_claims.title: Identifiers
source_claims.statement: Volumes can use human-readable labels and more fixed identifiers; serial numbers historically originated on mainframes and later supported media-change detection.

source_claims.title: FAT/NTFS labels and serials
source_claims.statement: FAT, NTFS, and exFAT impose different volume-label constraints; FAT/NTFS serial numbers support detection of volume replacement and formatting changes the serial.

misconception_corrections.misconception: A volume is always a physical disk.
misconception_corrections.correction: A volume is logical and may be partition-based, span media, or be packed in a file.

misconception_corrections.misconception: Every partition is automatically a usable volume.
misconception_corrections.correction: An OS can recognize a partition without recognizing its volume filesystem.

misconception_corrections.misconception: An ISO volume is a partition.
misconception_corrections.correction: The source treats an ISO9660 volume image as a file in a host volume, not a partition.

misconception_corrections.misconception: Windows and Unix-like systems expose volumes the same way.
misconception_corrections.correction: Windows uses drive letters/NTFS mount points; Unix-like systems graft volumes into a filesystem tree.

misconception_corrections.misconception: Moving a file always copies its data.
misconception_corrections.correction: Within one volume the move can be metadata-only; across volumes content must be copied.

misconception_corrections.misconception: A volume label is a permanent unique identifier.
misconception_corrections.correction: Labels are user-assignable; serial numbers provide a more fixed identifier.

misconception_corrections.misconception: Relabeling and formatting have the same identity effect.
misconception_corrections.correction: Formatting typically changes the serial; relabeling does not.

misconception_corrections.misconception: A volume has exactly one path.
misconception_corrections.correction: The source allows multiple path forms, including multiple drive letters via SUBST.

misconception_corrections.misconception: A drive letter identifies physical hardware directly.
misconception_corrections.correction: A drive letter identifies a logical volume in the OS namespace.

misconception_corrections.misconception: FAT, NTFS and exFAT use identical label constraints.
misconception_corrections.correction: The source gives different limits and character behavior for each.

fields.label: Core problem
fields.value: Coordinate desired software state across changing distributed compute infrastructure without requiring humans to manually orchestrate every machine and recovery action.

value.because: Controllers turn desired-state declarations into repeatable reconciliation loops.
Failure-induced divergence can trigger replacement/recovery actions.
Schedulers and workload controllers coordinate resource supply with workload demand.
A common API/object model abstracts workload management across machines, distributions and cloud environments.
CRDs, controllers, operators, scheduler extensions and CSI allow the platform to be adapted without changing the entire core.
The same declarative state model applies across workloads, networking, storage, configuration and infrastructure.

fields.label: Core problem
fields.value: Coordinate desired software state across changing distributed compute infrastructure without requiring humans to manually orchestrate every machine and recovery action.

value.because: Controllers turn desired-state declarations into repeatable reconciliation loops.
Failure-induced divergence can trigger replacement/recovery actions.
Schedulers and workload controllers coordinate resource supply with workload demand.
A common API/object model abstracts workload management across machines, distributions and cloud environments.
CRDs, controllers, operators, scheduler extensions and CSI allow the platform to be adapted without changing the entire core.
The same declarative state model applies across workloads, networking, storage, configuration and infrastructure.

fields.label: Central insight
fields.value: Kubernetes is best understood as a distributed control system and extensible API platform, not merely as a tool that 'runs containers'.

value.because: Controllers turn desired-state declarations into repeatable reconciliation loops.
